title: 2 Chronicles 17:1–19
context: 2 Chronicles 17:1–19 introduces the reign of Jehoshaphat son of Asa and has no parallel in Kings, which summarizes his reign briefly in 1 Kings 22:41–50. Jehoshaphat strengthens Judah, and the LORD is with him because he seeks the God of his father and walks in his commandments rather than in the ways of Israel. He removes high places and Asherah poles (17:6), though 20:33 says the high places were not taken away; interpreters discuss how the two statements relate, as the notes on 1 Kings 22:43 also observe, and this draft does not resolve the tension. In his third year he sends officials, Levites, and priests to teach in the cities of Judah with “the book of the LORD’s law” (17:9). The fear of the LORD keeps the surrounding kingdoms from war, tribute comes in, and the chapter closes with a muster of very large forces. The size of military numbers in Chronicles is discussed by interpreters, some of whom understand the word for thousand as a military unit; this draft records the figures as the WEB gives them. Both traditions read the chapter as shared ground: seeking the LORD and teaching his law lie at the root of Judah’s blessing.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place, and strengthened himself against Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat succeeds his father Asa and strengthens himself against Israel. The reign opens with defensive preparation against the northern kingdom.

Arminian readers note that strengthening the kingdom is a responsible use of the opportunities God gives, and they see a new king taking up his duties with prudence rather than presuming on God’s protection.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the hostility toward Israel at the start of the reign stands in tension with the alliance with Ahab in chapter 18, and they see the narrative preparing to show how a godly king can later be drawn into a harmful partnership.

Both traditions read the verse as narrative introduction and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: He placed forces in all the fortified cities of Judah, and set garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim, which Asa his father had taken.
verses.arminianNotes:
He places forces in all the fortified cities of Judah and garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa had taken.

Arminian readers see careful stewardship of the kingdom and note that faithfulness to God does not exclude wise planning for defense, since God commonly works through ordinary human diligence and foresight in the affairs of nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the reference to the cities Asa had taken (compare 15:8), and they see Jehoshaphat building on what God had already given through his father, so that the security of Judah rests on God’s continued favor.

Both traditions read the verse as historical description and as shared ground about responsible rule under God.

verses.text: The LORD was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the first ways of his father David, and didn’t seek the Baals,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD is with Jehoshaphat because he walks in the first ways of his father David and does not seek the Baals. The phrase about the first ways is often taken to mean David’s earlier years of faithfulness, though this is discussed.

Arminian readers note the explicit link between the king’s choices and the LORD’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the LORD being with the king is the decisive fact of the reign, and they see Jehoshaphat’s refusal to seek the Baals as the fruit of a heart God had turned toward himself.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: seeking the LORD rather than other gods is the root of a blessed reign in Chronicles.

verses.text: but sought the God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not in the ways of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
He seeks the God of his father, walks in his commandments, and does not follow the ways of Israel. The contrast with the northern kingdom is explicit.

Arminian readers see a king who chooses a different path from his neighbors, and they note that faithfulness involves real decisions to obey God when other models of kingship are close at hand and attractive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the language of seeking and walking as describing a whole life oriented toward God, and they note that Chronicles regularly connects such seeking with blessing, as the next verse shows.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about obedience and treat the contrast with Israel as part of the Chronicler’s theme of faithful worship.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD established the kingdom in his hand. All Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he had riches and honor in abundance.
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore the LORD establishes the kingdom in his hand. All Judah brings tribute, and he has riches and honor in abundance.

Arminian readers note the word therefore, which links the blessing to Jehoshaphat’s faithfulness, and they see God responding to obedience with real favor, while being careful not to make wealth a guaranteed reward for every believer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that it is the LORD who establishes the kingdom, so that the riches and honor are gifts of grace rather than earnings, and they note that the same riches will be mentioned again as the setting of the Ahab alliance (18:1).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s blessing on a faithful king.

verses.text: His heart was lifted up in the ways of the LORD. Furthermore, he took away the high places and the Asherah poles out of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
His heart is lifted up in the ways of the LORD, and he takes away the high places and the Asherah poles out of Judah. The later statement in 20:33 that the high places were not taken away stands in tension with this verse, and interpreters discuss how they relate.

Arminian readers see courage and zeal in reform.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the phrase about a lifted heart is used here in a good sense, of courage in the ways of the LORD, and they see reform as the outworking of a heart encouraged by God.

Both traditions note the tension with 20:33, which may reflect different kinds of high places or different stages of the reign, but they leave it unresolved and read the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: Also in the third year of his reign he sent his princes, even Ben Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah;
verses.arminianNotes:
In the third year of his reign he sends his princes, Ben Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah. Royal officials take part in teaching the people.

Arminian readers see the king taking responsibility for the people’s knowledge of God, so that each household can hear and respond to his law for itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the teaching mission reflects the conviction that true reform depends on God’s word being known, and that leaders are responsible to see that the people are instructed. This Micaiah is distinct from Micaiah son of Imla in chapter 18.

Both traditions read the teaching mission as shared ground and a model of reform rooted in Scripture.

verses.text: and with them Levites, even Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, the Levites; and with them Elishama and Jehoram, the priests.
verses.arminianNotes:
With the princes go Levites, Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, and the priests Elishama and Jehoram. The mission joins civil and religious leaders.

Arminian readers see many people sharing in the work of teaching, and they note that the spread of God’s word depends on the willing service of a wide circle of faithful people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Levites and priests were entrusted with teaching the law (compare Deuteronomy 33:10), and they see the mission as a proper use of the ministry God had appointed for instructing his people.

Both traditions read the list as shared ground and honor the named teachers whose work is otherwise unrecorded.

verses.text: They taught in Judah, having the book of the LORD’s law with them. They went about throughout all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
They teach in Judah, having “the book of the LORD’s law” with them, and go throughout all the cities of Judah teaching among the people. The text does not say exactly what the book contained.

Arminian readers see the people given real access to God’s word, so that they can understand his will and respond to it in faith and obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the teaching is anchored in a written book of the law, and they see the authority of Scripture as the foundation of reform rather than the king’s own ideas or the teachers’ opinions.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: knowing God’s word is central to the renewal of God’s people, and both avoid speculating about the book’s exact contents.

verses.text: The fear of the LORD fell on all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, so that they made no war against Jehoshaphat.
verses.arminianNotes:
The fear of the LORD falls on all the kingdoms around Judah, so that they make no war against Jehoshaphat. Peace follows the teaching mission.

Arminian readers note the sequence of faithful teaching followed by peace, and they see God honoring a people who seek to know and obey him, while recognizing that the text describes this reign rather than giving a rule for all times.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the fear comes from the LORD, so that Judah’s peace is his work among the nations rather than the result of military strength alone, and they see God protecting his people for his name’s sake.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the LORD’s rule over the surrounding kingdoms.

verses.text: Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents and silver for tribute. The Arabians also brought him flocks: seven thousand seven hundred rams and seven thousand seven hundred male goats.
verses.arminianNotes:
Some of the Philistines bring presents and silver as tribute, and the Arabians bring seven thousand seven hundred rams and seven thousand seven hundred male goats. Neighboring peoples acknowledge Judah’s strength.

Arminian readers see the outward signs of a blessed reign and note that God’s favor on Judah becomes visible to those around them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the tribute from former enemies such as the Philistines shows the LORD subduing the nations around his people, a theme that recalls the reigns of David and Solomon.

Both traditions read the verse as historical description of God’s blessing, and they treat the numbers as recorded without building doctrine on them.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat grew great exceedingly; and he built fortresses and store cities in Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat grows exceedingly great and builds fortresses and store cities in Judah. His reign prospers.

Arminian readers see the king using his prosperity for the good of the kingdom, and they note that faithful leaders are called to steward blessings wisely rather than to consume them for their own glory or comfort.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that greatness here is presented as the LORD’s gift to a king who sought him, and they observe that the narrative will soon show how even great blessing can become the setting for an unwise decision (18:1).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s blessing and the responsibility that comes with it.

verses.text: He had many works in the cities of Judah; and men of war, mighty men of valor, in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
He has many works in the cities of Judah and men of war, mighty men of valor, in Jerusalem. The kingdom is both productive and secure.

Arminian readers see diligent administration that serves the people, and they note that the Chronicler presents such activity positively when it flows from a heart that seeks the LORD rather than from pride or self-reliance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the strength of Judah as the outward form of the LORD’s establishing of the kingdom (17:5), and they note that the coming crisis of chapter 20 will show that Judah’s safety finally rests on God and not on soldiers.

Both traditions read the verse as historical description and as shared ground.

verses.text: This was the numbering of them according to their fathers’ houses: From Judah, the captains of thousands: Adnah the captain, and with him three hundred thousand mighty men of valor;
verses.arminianNotes:
The muster by fathers’ houses begins: from Judah, the captains of thousands, with Adnah the captain and three hundred thousand mighty men of valor. The size of such figures is discussed by interpreters, some of whom take the word for thousand as a military unit.

Arminian readers note that the record presents an organized and capable army.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the precise meaning of the numbers does not affect the point of the passage, which is that the LORD has made Judah strong, and they decline to settle the question by conjecture.

Both traditions record the figures as the WEB gives them, hold the interpretive question open, and treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: and next to him Jehohanan the captain, and with him two hundred eighty thousand;
verses.arminianNotes:
Next to Adnah is Jehohanan the captain, with two hundred eighty thousand. The list continues by commander.

Arminian readers see named leaders entrusted with responsibility, and they note that the Chronicler honors those who served faithfully in the defense of God’s people, even when little else is recorded about them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the orderly arrangement of the army as part of the picture of a kingdom established by God, and they observe that the list prepares for the later contrast in chapter 20, when Judah wins without fighting.

Both traditions read the verse as historical record and leave the questions about the size of the numbers open.

verses.text: and next to him Amasiah the son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself to the LORD, and with him two hundred thousand mighty men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Next is Amasiah son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself to the LORD, with two hundred thousand mighty men of valor. He alone in the list receives a comment about his devotion.

Arminian readers highlight the willing offering of himself, and they see a model of free and wholehearted devotion that God honors.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers agree that Amasiah’s willing self-offering is commended, and they see such willingness as the fruit of God’s work in the heart (compare Psalm 110:3, where the people offer themselves willingly); the related question treated in the existing box at Psalm 110:3 is not reopened here.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: willing devotion to the LORD is praised, and both see it as a model for service.

verses.text: From Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, and with him two hundred thousand armed with bow and shield;
verses.arminianNotes:
From Benjamin comes Eliada, a mighty man of valor, with two hundred thousand armed with bow and shield. Benjamin stands alongside Judah in the southern kingdom.

Arminian readers note the inclusion of Benjamin and see a united people in Judah, and they observe that the Chronicler takes care to record the contribution of each part of the kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Benjamin’s place with Judah reflects the division of the kingdom after Solomon (compare 11:1), and they see God preserving a people around the house of David.

Both traditions read the verse as historical record, treat the numbers as recorded, and find no point of doctrinal division here.

verses.text: and next to him Jehozabad, and with him one hundred eighty thousand ready and prepared for war.
verses.arminianNotes:
Next is Jehozabad, with one hundred eighty thousand ready and prepared for war. The muster ends with readiness.

Arminian readers see preparation as responsible leadership, and they note that readiness for danger is not opposed to trust in God, since the faithful king plans wisely while still depending on the LORD for victory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the record of great forces sets up the striking contrast of chapter 20, where Jehoshaphat confesses that Judah has no might against the invaders and the LORD alone wins the battle.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about preparation held under dependence on God.

verses.text: These were those who waited on the king, in addition to those whom the king put in the fortified cities throughout all Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
These are those who wait on the king, in addition to those he places in the fortified cities throughout Judah. The chapter closes with the king’s strength fully displayed.

Arminian readers see the summary as showing how much God had entrusted to Jehoshaphat, and they note that great resources bring great responsibility for how they are used.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the chapter moves from seeking God (17:3–4) to strength and wealth, and that Chronicles will immediately test whether the king’s strength leads him to rely on God or on alliances (18:1).

Both traditions read the verse as a summary of God’s blessing and treat it as shared ground.
